blocks.c: Chapter Nine: Dov's Arithmetic
Dov Ilesca did his best thinking upside down, which was inconvenient for everyone.

Sol found him that night in the frame-space under the gallery, hanging by his knees from a cross-member with a slate on his chest and chalk dust in his eyebrows, in the manner of a bat that had taken up accountancy.
"The blood goes to your head," she said.
"That's the idea. Hold the lamp. Higher. There." He wrote something, rubbed it out, wrote it again. "Right. I know how much they're taking."
Sol sat down on a bracket. "Go on."

"Eleven parts in a hundred is one bell in nine, agreed? That's if a bell goes fully dead and nothing else changes. But when the Ninth went dead on us we lost two spans, then six. Two is less than eleven parts of forty. Six is more. That bothered me for eleven days and now it doesn't, and the reason it doesn't is that I was doing the sum for a bell that had stopped, and the bell hasn't stopped. It's ringing. Somebody else is spending it."
"Spending."

"Carry isn't a thing the bell makes. Everyone says that and everyone is wrong, including me until Tuesday. The bell doesn't make carry, the bell holds a note, and the note is a claim on the air. If two bells hold the same note, the air has to decide which claim it honours, and it honours the one that's rung truer, and truer is a technical word and I have spent three days finding out that it means: rung closer to the interval." He tapped the slate. "Four beats. We ring four beats between strikes because that's the tradition. The tradition is wrong. Or rather it's rounded. The true interval on a melt-sixty-two bell is four beats and about a tenth."
Sol's stomach did something unpleasant. "You're saying they're ringing better than us."

"I'm saying they're ringing exactly, and we're ringing approximately, and they've had eleven years to practise." He unhooked his knees and came down in a controlled fall that Sol had learned not to react to. "Here's the shape of it. Look."
He held the slate to the lamp.

items: Eleven times in eleven years the Ninth went fully dead for one round. Those are the days they rang a full sequence — took everything.

Every other day of those eleven years, our tally says the Ninth hummed full, and it did hum full, to any ear on this ship except one. But the carry has been down by about a part in a hundred the whole time, which shows up nowhere except in coal.

Coal. The Gull has burned four per cent more coal per crossing since the refit, every crossing, for eleven years, because a ship carrying less carry sits lower and drags more. Halloway has the coal ledgers. Nobody ever put the coal ledger next to the tally because they live in different offices.
One part in a hundred, taken continuously, for eleven years, is an enormous amount of carry, and it did not go into the air. It went into holding something up.

blocks.c: "How big a something?" said Sol.
Dov wiped the slate with his sleeve and drew a rectangle.

"That's the Gull. Forty spans of carry, eight hundred tons, four hundred and eleven passengers and change." He drew a second rectangle beside it, a third the size. "That's what one part in a hundred, banked for eleven years and topped up eleven times, will hold at low altitude in still air, and I have checked it twice and I do not want to have checked it right."
Sol looked at the little chalk box.
"That's not a bell in a shed," she said.
"No."
"That's a town."

They took it to Halloway, because everything went to Halloway now, and the purser listened to the whole of it with his hands folded and then did the single most frightening thing Sol saw anybody do that month, which was to get out the coal ledgers without being asked.
"You wish to know," he said, "whether the four per cent is real."
"Yes."

"It is real. I have known it was real for nine years and I have written four memoranda about it, and each of those memoranda came back from the Ridge with a note saying that fuel efficiency on the Antrell run had declined in line with fleet averages." He pulled a bound quarto out of the case. "Which is true. It has. Because every ship on this run passes north of the Quiet."
Dov stopped with his chalk halfway to the slate.
"Every ship."

"Four ships. The Gull, the Cormorant, the Sabine Rey and the mail-packet." Halloway licked his thumb and turned pages. "Fleet average went up four per cent in the year after the Gull's refit and has stayed there. Everybody assumed it was the price of coal, or the age of the frames, or the weather, because when everybody's number moves at once nobody looks for a thief. They look for a season."
"But it's only us," said Sol. "It's only our bell that's paired."
"It is only your bell that is paired," Halloway agreed. "So either the fleet average moved for a different reason at exactly the same time — "
" — or she's taking it off all four," said Dov, in a small voice, "and only ours has a twin, so only ours shows in the tally."
The purser closed the ledger.

"I have been a clerk for forty-one years," he said. "I will tell you the worst thing I know about numbers, which is this: a figure that has been wrong for a long time stops being an error and becomes a baseline, and then it is defended. Four per cent has been in the Company's budget for eleven years. It is in the fares. It is in my own salary. If we prove where it went, we do not merely embarrass a commission. We take four per cent away from eleven people who have grown used to it."
